Ghetto of Pitigliano

Museum · Pitigliano, Italy

The Jewish Ghetto of Pitigliano is the historic center of the town’s Jewish community, which flourished for centuries alongside its Catholic neighbors and earned Pitigliano the name “Little Jerusalem.”

Established in the early 17th century, the ghetto was once locked at night. Because space within its boundaries was limited, residents expanded underground, carving rooms into the town’s soft volcanic tufa rock. These subterranean spaces included a mikveh, a kosher wine cellar, a ritual slaughterhouse, and an oven used to bake unleavened bread for Passover.

A distinctive local reminder of this history is the *sfratto*, a traditional Jewish biscuit filled with nuts and honey. Its name means “eviction” in Italian, and its stick-like shape recalls the batons once used to force Jewish residents into the ghetto.
